records.summary: The model is understandable only if execution evidence, protected-data boundaries and executor-independent work are made explicit; adjacent tooling is secondary.

items.label: Execution history
items.reason: The central production argument depends on being able to reconstruct consequential work after it happened.

items.label: Protected data separation
items.reason: The control layer is incomplete if observing orchestration implicitly grants broad access to protected business data.

items.label: Human-agent task equivalence
items.reason: Executor-independent tasks make escalation and handoff understandable without turning human review into an unrelated exception process.

records.summary: Temporal becomes coherent only when Workflow Execution, Event History and Activity retry semantics are understood as separate responsibilities.

items.label: Workflow Execution
items.reason: The reader needs a stable unit of long-running orchestration before Worker failure and recovery can make sense.

items.label: Event History
items.reason: Durable recovery depends on understanding where workflow progress is represented independently of one Worker process.

items.label: Activity execution
items.reason: Side-effecting work must be separated from deterministic orchestration to understand retry behavior and failure boundaries.

items.label: Idempotency under retry
items.reason: The practical boundary of durable execution is missed if repeated external effects are assumed to become exactly-once automatically.

records.summary: OPA needs two prerequisites: policy as explicit decision logic and a clear boundary between deciding permission and enforcing the protected action.

items.label: Policy as code
items.reason: OPA only makes sense once policy is treated as explicit, reviewable decision logic rather than hidden application branching.

items.label: Policy decision / enforcement separation
items.reason: The architecture is misread if the policy engine is treated as the component that performs the protected business action.

items.label: Policy distribution
items.reason: Operational use becomes clearer when policy and data lifecycle are separated from application deployment through bundles or equivalent mechanisms.

records.summary: ReAct requires a compact loop model first; production governance is useful boundary context but is not a prerequisite for understanding the paper mechanism itself.

items.label: ReAct loop
items.reason: The paper's mechanism is the repeated relationship between reasoning, environment action and returned observation.

items.label: Reasoning trace
items.reason: A reasoning step must be distinguished from an external action because only the latter changes or queries the environment.

items.label: Observation grounding
items.reason: The value of acting is not only execution; returned evidence changes what the model can reason about next.

items.label: Controlled execution
items.reason: This prior model is useful for separating ReAct's cognitive loop from authorization, durability and outcome verification in production.

records.summary: The source needs only the retrieval event and the immediate-versus-delayed distinction; broader learning-science machinery would add noise at this stage.

items.label: Retrieval practice
items.reason: The testing effect cannot be understood unless retrieval is treated as a learning event rather than only an assessment event.

items.label: Immediate performance / delayed retention gap
items.reason: The study's central result depends on ranking learning conditions differently immediately and after a meaningful delay.

items.label: Metacognitive confidence gap
items.reason: Confidence matters as a secondary concept because feeling fluent immediately can diverge from what is retrievable later.

records.summary: The controller model needs only three tightly related pieces before the larger implications make sense: the reconciliation loop itself, a declared desired state and feedback about observed state.

items.label: Reconciliation loop
items.reason: The source is fundamentally about repeated comparison and correction rather than one-shot procedural execution.

items.label: Desired state
items.reason: A controller cannot reconcile anything unless there is an explicit target condition separate from current reality.

items.label: Observed state
items.reason: Feedback about actual state is what lets the controller decide whether the target has drifted and whether corrective work is needed.

records.summary: The pattern is easiest to understand by starting from the existing retry-idempotency problem, then adding the source's two concrete pieces: a receiver that remembers prior requests and a stable identity for the logical operation.

items.label: Idempotency under retry
items.reason: The receiver pattern solves a concrete instance of the broader problem that retrying a side effect must not create an unintended duplicate outcome.

items.label: Idempotent Receiver
items.reason: The receiver-side lookup and response-reuse behavior is the concrete mechanism introduced by the source.

items.label: Logical request identity
items.reason: Without a stable identity reused by retries, the receiver cannot know whether a delivery represents the same intended operation or a new one.

records.summary: Three concepts are sufficient for the first mental model: append-first WAL commit, checkpointing as a separate consolidation step, and the reader end-mark snapshot that makes concurrent reads understandable.

items.label: Write-ahead log
items.reason: The inversion from overwriting the database to appending committed changes is the central storage mechanism.

items.label: Checkpointing
items.reason: The model is incomplete if append-only commit is understood without the later operation that consolidates WAL pages into the database.

items.label: WAL reader snapshot
items.reason: The reader end mark is what makes stable reads alongside newer appended commits coherent.

records.summary: The MVCC model is coherent once the reader understands the multiversion model, the snapshot that controls visibility, the isolation rule that scopes that snapshot, and why stronger guarantees can intentionally fail a transaction.

items.label: Multiversion Concurrency Control (MVCC)
items.reason: The core concurrency benefit depends on separating visible row versions from one universally current physical value.

items.label: MVCC snapshot
items.reason: Snapshot visibility is the concrete mechanism that lets a statement or transaction read a coherent database version while commits continue.

items.label: Transaction isolation scope
items.reason: Read Committed and Repeatable Read are easy to confuse unless snapshot lifetime is treated as an explicit part of the isolation contract.

items.label: Serialization failure and retry
items.reason: The strongest consistency story is incomplete unless transaction abort and whole-transaction retry are understood as expected concurrency behavior.

records.summary: The mental model needs three pieces: the in-process deployment boundary, the embedded query-engine composition pattern, and direct file querying as one concrete leverage point.

items.label: In-process analytical database
items.reason: Without the deployment boundary, DuckDB looks like just another SQL database rather than a different composition model.

items.label: Embedded query engine
items.reason: This concept explains how host application code invokes analytics directly instead of through a separate database-service hop.

items.label: Direct file querying
items.reason: It is the most concrete example of how embedding can remove an intermediate ingestion boundary from a local data workflow.
